slides.notes: In this unit, we will begin by examining the concept of a tissue in general, and then we will move on to an examination of the four major tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue.

slides.body:
Part 1. Tissue: a higher level of organization

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Let’s begin with Part 1. Tissue: a higher level of organization.

slides.title: Part 1. Tissue: a higher level of organization
slides.body:
Part 1. Tissue: a higher level of organization

Tissues – cells organized into functional groups 
e.g., neurons lumped together for quick communication
4 tissue types:
epithelial

connective

muscle

Four Types of Tissue: Body. The four types of tissues are exemplified in nervous tissue, stratified squamous epithelial tissue, cardiac muscle tissue, and connective tissue in small intestine. Clockwise from nervous tissue, LM × 872, LM × 282, LM × 460, LM × 800. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
During the last unit, we discussed cells, as well as cell differentiation into different cell types. As a result of that process, your body contains hundreds of different cell types. However, these cells are not randomly scattered throughout your body. Instead, they are found within organized groupings called tissues. The pattern of arrangement of cells within a tissue reflect the tissue’s functions. Having cells of different types arranged next to one another helps to increase efficiency and speed of activity. For example, clumping the brain’s neurons together allows for quicker decision-making, which can be essential for survival, than if those neurons were dispersed across your entire body. 

Although there are many types of cells in the human body, they are organized into four broad categories of tissues: epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous.

Epithelial tissue (also referred to as the epithelium) refers to the sheets of cells that cover exterior surfaces of the body, line internal cavities and passageways, and form certain glands. 

Connective tissue, as its name implies, binds the cells and organs of the body together and functions in the protection, support, and integration of all parts of the body. 

Muscle tissue is excitable, responding to stimulation and contracting to provide movement. It occurs as three major types: skeletal muscle, smooth muscle, and cardiac muscle. The latter in the heart. 

Nervous tissue is also excitable, allowing the propagation of electrochemical signals in the form of nerve impulses that communicate between different regions of the body.

A disruption of the structure of any of these tissues is a sign of injury or disease. Such changes can be detected through histology, the microscopic study of tissue appearance, organization, and function.

Part 2. Epithelial tissue

Epithelium
sheets of cells covering body surfaces
Endothelium

e.g., blood vessels
Glands

Microscopic anatomy of an artery. Credit: en:User:Stijn Ghesquiere, user:Drsrisenthil, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Most epithelial tissues are essentially large sheets of cells covering the surfaces of the body, lining the outside of organs, and lining the insides of body cavities. 

Epithelium also forms much of the glandular tissue of the body. Skin is not the only area of the body exposed to the outside. Other areas include the airways, the digestive tract, as well as the urinary and reproductive systems, all of which are lined by an epithelium. Hollow organs and body cavities that do not connect to the exterior of the body, which includes, blood vessels and serous membranes, are lined by endothelium, which is a type of epithelium.

slides.title: Part 2. Epithelial tissue
slides.body:
Part 2. Epithelial tissue

Epithelial tissues:
highly cellular = little extracellular material present between cells
polarity: apical (exposed surface) & basal (underlying side)
some organelles segregated to basal side
others, like cilia or microvilli are on apical side

apical

basal

Goblet cell in GI and respiratory tracts secrete mucus. Credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Stratified squamous epithelium.
slides.notes: All epithelia share some important structural and functional features. First of all, epithelial tissue is highly cellular, meaning that there is little or no extracellular material present between cells. The epithelial cells also exhibit polarity, so that there are differences in structure and function between the exposed or apical surface and the basal surface that is on the side of the underlying body structures. Certain organelles are segregated to the basal sides, whereas other organelles and extensions, such as cilia, when present, are on the apical surface.

slides.title: Part 2. Epithelial tissue
slides.body:
Part 2. Epithelial tissue

Epithelial tissues:
attached to underlying connective tissues via basement membrane:
basal lamina - mixture of glycoproteins and collagen protein fibres
attached to reticular lamina (reticular fibres secreted by the underlying connective tissue)
nearly avascular (no blood vessels present)
nutrient & waste exchange occurs with diffusion from underlying layers or surface
many are rapidly replaceable - dead surface cells continually slough off of the skin, airways, and digestive tracts

apical

Basement 
membrane
(basal lamina +
reticular lamina)

basal

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Stratified squamous epithelium.
slides.notes:
The basal lamina, a mixture of glycoproteins and collagen produced by the epithelial cells, provides an attachment site for the epithelium, separating it from underlying connective tissue. The basal lamina attaches to a reticular lamina, which is secreted by the underlying connective tissue, forming a basement membrane that helps hold it all together.

Epithelial tissues are also nearly avascular. No blood vessels cross the basement membrane to enter the tissue, and nutrients must come by diffusion or absorption from underlying tissues or the surface. Many epithelial tissues are capable of rapidly replacing damaged and dead surface cells that continually slough off of the skin, airways, and digestive tracts.

slides.title: Part 2. Epithelial tissue
slides.body:
Part 2. Epithelial tissue

Protection
body’s first line of protection from physical, chemical, and biological wear and tear
Absorption
for substances to truly enter body, they have to be absorbed across an epithelial cell
Secretion
various epithelial cells secrete substances
e.g., mucus, enzymes, HCl

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Parietal cell. Credit: MustafaSalahalden, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes:
Epithelial tissues provide the body’s first line of protection from physical, chemical, and biological wear and tear. The cells of an epithelium also act as gatekeepers, controlling permeability and allowing for the selective transfer of materials into the body—all substances that actually enter the body (that is are actually absorbed, and do not just enter a canal like the digestive tract) must cross an epithelium. 

Many epithelial cells are also capable of secretion. They release mucus to moisten and lubricate apical surfaces, as well as various other chemical compounds for various purposes. The epithelium of the small intestine releases digestive enzymes, for example. Cells lining the respiratory tract secrete mucus that traps incoming microorganisms and particles. Glandular epithelial cells of the stomach, like the one in this figure, also release hydrochloric acid, HCl, which in liquid dissociates into hydrogen and chloride ions.

Types of Epithelial Tissue. Simple epithelial tissue is organized as a single layer of cells and stratified epithelial tissue is formed by several layers of cells. Pseudostratified epithelial tissue is a single layer of cells that appear to be multiple layers because of the position of their nuclei. Epithelial tissue is further defined by the shape of the apical layer of cells in the tissue.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Epithelial tissues are classified according to the shape of the cells, and according to the number of cell layers. 

Cell shapes can be squamous (flat and thin), cuboidal (boxy, each as wide as it is tall), or columnar (rectangular, taller than wide). 

Similarly, the number of cell layers in the tissue can be one—where every cell rests on the basal lamina—which is termed a simple epithelium. In contrast, more than one layer of cells is classified as stratified epithelium. In stratified epithelium, only the basal layer of cells rests on the basal lamina. Another specialized type of epithelium, pseudostratified, describes tissue with a single layer of irregularly shaped cells that give the appearance of more than one layer (note that pseudo- means “false”). 

Let’s look at combinations of these shapes and layers in more detail…

slides.title: Part 2. Epithelial tissue
slides.body:
Part 2. Epithelial tissue

Simple squamous
rapid exchange

secretion

Simple columnar
secretion

ciliated columnar epithelium moves along particulate matter in respiratory & reproductive tracts

Summary of Epithelial Tissue Types. Different types of epithelial tissue serve different functions and are found in different locations in the body.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The shape of the cells in the single cell layer of simple epithelium reflects the function of those cells. The cells in simple squamous epithelium have the appearance of thin scales, as do their nuclei within them. Because of the thinness of these cells, simple squamous epithelium is present where rapid exchange of chemical compounds is observed. For example, the alveoli of lungs and the lining of blood capillaries are both made up of simple squamous epithelium to facilitate rapid exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

In simple cuboidal epithelium, the nucleus appears round and is generally located near the center of the cell. These epithelia are active in the secretion and absorption of molecules. Simple cuboidal epithelia are observed in the lining of the kidney tubules, where substances are both secreted and reabsorbed, and in the ducts of glands.

In simple columnar epithelium, the nucleus of the tall column-like cells tends to also match the cell’s shape—here it is elongated; it is also located in the basal end of the cell. Like the cuboidal epithelia, this epithelium is active in the absorption and secretion of molecules. Simple columnar epithelium forms the lining of some sections of the digestive system and parts of the female reproductive tract. Ciliated columnar epithelium is composed of simple columnar epithelial cells with cilia on their apical surfaces. These epithelial cells are found in the lining of the uterine tubes and parts of the respiratory system, where the beating of the cilia helps remove particulate matter.

Stratified squamous

Stratified cuboidal

Summary of Epithelial Tissue Types. Different types of epithelial tissue serve different functions and are found in different locations in the body.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A stratified epithelium consists of several stacked layers of cells. This epithelium protects against physical and chemical wear and tear. The stratified epithelium is named by the shape of the most apical layer of cells, closest to the open space.

Stratified squamous epithelium is the most common type of stratified epithelium in the human body. The apical cells are squamous, whereas the basal layer contains either columnar or cuboidal cells. The top layer may be covered with dead cells filled with keratin. Mammalian skin is an example of this dry, keratinized, stratified squamous epithelium. The lining of the mouth cavity is an example of a nonkeratinized, stratified squamous epithelium. Stratified cuboidal epithelium and stratified columnar epithelium can also be found in certain glands and ducts, but are relatively uncommon in the body.

slides.title: Part 2. Epithelial tissue
slides.body:
Part 2. Epithelial tissue

Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
all cells are in contact with basal lamina, though not all reach apical surface
secretion and movement of mucus
found in respiratory tract
cilia help move particulate matter out to where they can be coughed out or swallowed

Summary of Epithelial Tissue Types. Different types of epithelial tissue serve different functions and are found in different locations in the body.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium appears to be stratified but instead consists of a single layer of irregularly shaped and differently sized columnar cells. In pseudostratified epithelium, nuclei of neighbouring cells appear at different levels rather than clustered in the basal end. This arrangement gives the appearance of stratification; but in fact, all the cells are in contact with the basal lamina, although some do not reach the apical surface. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is found in the respiratory tract, where some of these cells have cilia, which again help to move particulate matter out to where they can be coughed out or swallowed.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Transitional epithelium describes a form of specialized stratified epithelium in which the shape of the cells can vary. It is found only in the urinary system and allows for the gradual changes in the shapes of the apical cells as the bladder fills with urine.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue

Part 3. Connective tissue

Connective tissues connect tissues and organs
Connective tissues contain:
cells
matrix:
ground substance 
the major part of matrix
usually fluid but in bones, is mineralized and solid

Extracellular matrix of loose connective tissue. Credit: Sagearbor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As its name depicts, one of the major functions of connective tissue is to connect tissues and organs. Unlike epithelial tissue, which is composed of cells closely packed with little or no extracellular space in between, connective tissue cells are dispersed in a matrix. 

The matrix usually includes a large amount of extracellular material produced by the connective tissue cells that are embedded within it. The major component of the matrix is a ground substance. This ground substance is usually a fluid, but it can also be mineralized and solid, as in bones. Connective tissues also usually contain protein fibres.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Connective tissues categorized by ground substance & fibre: 
connective tissue proper
protein fibres in viscous ground substance
loose connective tissue
dense connective tissue
supportive connective tissue
fibres in denser matrix; calcified in bone
bone
cartilage
fluid connective tissue
watery fluid containing salts, nutrients, and dissolved proteins
lymph
blood

Connective tissue examples

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The three broad categories of connective tissue are classified according to the characteristics of their ground substance and the types of fibres found within the matrix. These categories can be found in the table on this slide. 

Connective tissue proper includes loose connective tissue and dense connective tissue. Both tissues have a variety of cell types and protein fibres suspended in a viscous ground substance. Dense connective tissue is reinforced by bundles of fibres that provide tensile strength, elasticity, and protection. In loose connective tissue, the fibres are loosely organized, leaving large spaces in between. 

Supportive connective tissue – bone and cartilage – provide structure and strength to the body and protect soft tissues. A few distinct cell types and densely packed fibres in a matrix characterize these tissues. In bone, the matrix is rigid and described as calcified because of the deposited calcium salts. 

In fluid connective tissue – lymph and blood – various specialized cells circulate in a watery fluid containing salts, nutrients, and dissolved proteins.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Connective tissues functions
connect & support: e.g., connective tissue sheaths, tendons
protection: e.g., leukocytes (white blood cells), adipose tissue (thermal & impact)
transport: e.g., blood and lymph
energy storage: adipose tissue

A skeletal muscle attached to bone via a tendon. Credit: http://training.seer.cancer.gov/module_anatomy/unit4_2_muscle_structure.html, CC Public Domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Blood cells. Credit: Rozzychan, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Connective tissues perform many functions in the body, but most importantly, they connect and support other tissues. Examples include the connective tissue sheath that surrounds muscles and muscle cells, the tendons that attach muscles to bones, and the bones of the skeleton that allow for changes of body position. 

Protection is another major function of connective tissue. Some connective tissues overlay and protect delicate organs. Specialized white blood cells defend the body from pathogens. 

Another function of connective tissues is transport. Transport of fluid, nutrients, wastes, and chemical messengers is ensured by specialized fluid connective tissues, such as blood and lymph. 

Adipose cells (commonly called fat cells) store surplus energy in the form of fat and contribute to the thermal insulation of the body, as well as cushioning from physical impact.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Connective tissue proper – cells:
fibroblasts - cells that secrete protein fibers and matrix into the extracellular space
adipocytes - cells that store lipids as droplets in cytoplasm
mesenchymal cells - multipotent adult stem cells; can become any connective tissue 
macrophages - phagocytotic white blood cells; enter matrix from blood
mast cells - release histamine, causing vasodilation & thus increased blood flow at site of injury

Connective Tissue Proper. Fibroblasts produce this fibrous tissue. Connective tissue proper includes the fixed cells fibrocytes, adipocytes, and mesenchymal cells. LM × 400. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Let’s now look at some of these types of connective tissues, in more detail.

We’ll start with Connective Tissue Proper, and the types of cells that can be found within it.

Fibroblasts are cells that secrete protein fibers and matrix into the extracellular space. Fibroblast are present in all connective tissue proper. 

Adipocytes are cells that store lipids as droplets, and those droplets fill most of their cytoplasm. 

Mesenchymal cells are multipotent adult stem cells. These cells can differentiate into any type of connective tissue cells needed for repair and healing of damaged tissue. 

Macrophages are a large type of phagocytotic white blood cell, which enters the connective tissue matrix from blood vessels. 

Mast cells (not shown in the figure) are also found in connective tissue proper. When the tissue is irritated or damaged, mast cells release the signaling molecule histamine, which causes vasodilation, or enlargement of blood vessels, and thus increased blood flow at a site of injury or infection, along with the itching, swelling, and redness that you recognize as an allergic response.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Connective tissue proper – 3 types of protein fibres:
collagen fibres – flexible but high tensile strength; e.g., in tendons & ligaments – allow movement
elastic fibres – recoil after stretch; e.g., in skin and elastic ligaments of vertebral column
reticular fibres – narrow, branching; e.g., in soft organs, support parenchyma (functional tissue of organs)
All these fibres are embedded in ground substance – clear, viscous, colorless matrix containing of polysaccharides and proteins

Connective Tissue Proper. Fibroblasts produce this fibrous tissue. Connective tissue proper includes the fixed cells fibrocytes, adipocytes, and mesenchymal cells. LM × 400. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Within the connective tissue proper, there exist three main types of fibres that are secreted by fibroblasts: collagen fibres, elastic fibres, and reticular fibres. 

Collagen fibres, while flexible, have great tensile strength, resist stretching, and give ligaments and tendons their characteristic resilience and strength. These fibres hold connective tissues together, even during the movement of the body. 

Elastic fibres, after being stretched or compressed, will return to their original shape. Elastic fibres are prominent in elastic tissues found in skin and the elastic ligaments of the vertebral column. 

Reticular fibres are narrow and are arrayed in a branching network. They are found throughout the body, but are most abundant in the reticular tissue of soft organs, such as liver and spleen, where they anchor and provide structural support to the parenchyma (the functional, rather than connective or supportive cells, of glands and organs). 

All of these fibre types are embedded in ground substance, a clear, viscous, colorless matrix made of polysaccharides and proteins, forming the extracellular matrix.

slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Loose areolar connective tissue. Credit: Berkshire Community College  Bioscience Image Library, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Connective tissue proper
loose connective tissue*
less collagen present, so stretchy
between organs – acts to absorb shock and bind tissues together
allows water, salts, & nutrients to diffuse through to adjacent cells
areolar
“general/non-specialized”, widespread, underlies epithelia, supports organs, surrounds blood vessels & muscle fibres
adipose
adipose cells, highly vascularized for fat transport, fat storage, temperature regulation, protection from mechanical injury
reticular (“little net”)

*some use “loose connective tissue” interchangeably with “areolar tissue”; view adipose & reticular as separate

Adipose Tissue. This is a loose connective tissue that consists of fat cells with little extracellular matrix. It stores fat for energy and provides insulation. LM × 800. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

Reticular Tissue. This is a loose connective tissue made up of a network of reticular fibres that provides a supportive framework for soft organs. LM × 1600. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical school © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
First, let’s look at types of loose connective tissue. This type of tissue is found between many organs where it acts both to absorb shock and bind tissues together. It allows water, salts, and various nutrients to diffuse through to adjacent or embedded cells and tissues. 

According to some views, loose connective tissue is really a misnomer, and loose connective tissue is just areolar tissue, while adipose and reticular are separate types of connective tissues. So, we may use the two terms somewhat interchangeably in this course. 

Areolar tissue is connective tissues that shows little specialization. It contains all the cell types and fibres previously described and is distributed in a random, web-like fashion. It fills the spaces between muscle fibres, surrounds blood and lymph vessels, and supports organs in the abdominal cavity. Areolar tissue underlies most epithelia and represents the connective tissue component of epithelial membranes, which are described further in a later section. You can think of it as a generalist, in terms of function.

Adipose tissue is much more specialized and consists mostly of fat storage cells, with little extracellular matrix. A large number of capillaries allow rapid storage and mobilization of lipid molecules. As mentioned earlier, these adipose, or fat cells, contribute mostly to lipid storage, but they also serve as insulation from cold temperatures and from mechanical injuries.

Reticular tissue is a mesh-like, supportive framework for soft organs such as lymphatic tissue, the spleen, and the liver. Reticular cells produce the reticular fibres that form the network onto which other cells attach. It derives its name from the Latin reticulus, which means “little net.”

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Connective tissue proper
dense connective tissue (a.k.a., fibrous connective tissue)
more collagen fibres than loose; hence does not stretch readily
dense regular
dense & parallel collagen fibres; strong in direction of fibres
e.g., tendons, ligaments
dense irregular
fibers at random angles OR layers of parallel fibers at different angles
e.g., dermis of skin
elastic
elastic versions of both regular and irregular exist
contain collagen AND elastin fibres
elastin helps recoil to original shape
e.g., vocal folds, vertebral ligaments

Figure 7. Dense Connective Tissue. (a) Dense regular connective tissue consists of collagenous fibres packed into parallel bundles. (b) Dense irregular connective tissue consists of collagenous fibres interwoven into a mesh-like network. From top, LM × 1000, LM × 200. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Dense connective tissue (also called fibrous connective tissue) contains more collagen fibres than does loose connective tissue. As a consequence, it displays greater resistance to stretching. There are two major categories of dense connective tissue: regular and irregular. 

Dense regular connective tissue fibres are parallel to each other, enhancing tensile strength and resistance to stretching in the direction of the fibre orientations. Ligaments and tendons are made of dense regular connective tissue, but in ligaments not all fibres are parallel. Dense regular elastic connective tissue contains elastin fibres in addition to collagen fibres, which allows the ligament to return to its original length after stretching. The ligaments in the vocal folds and between the vertebrae in the vertebral column are elastic.

In dense irregular connective tissue, the direction of fibres is random. This arrangement gives the tissue greater strength in all directions and less strength in one particular direction. In some tissues, fibres crisscross and form a mesh. In other tissues, stretching in several directions is achieved by alternating layers where fibres run in the same orientation in each layer, and it is the layers themselves that are stacked at an angle. The dermis of the skin is an example of dense irregular connective tissue rich in collagen fibres. Dense irregular elastic connective tissue give arterial walls the strength and the ability to regain original shape after stretching.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Supportive connective tissue
two major forms: cartilage and bone
allow body to maintain posture and protect internal organs

Connective tissue examples

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Okay, so that was connective tissue proper. Now let’s turn to supportive connective tissue. Two major forms of supportive connective tissue, cartilage and bone, allow the body to maintain its posture and protect internal organs.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Supportive connective tissue
cartilage
polysaccharides bind with ground substance proteins to form the extracellular matrix
embedded in matrix are chondrocytes (cartilage cells); spaces they occupy are called lacunae (singular = lacuna)
perichondrium - layer of dense irregular connective tissue encapsulating the cartilage
cartilaginous tissue is avascular
all nutrients need to diffuse to it, through the matrix - thus slow healing

Cartilage

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The distinctive appearance of cartilage is due to polysaccharides, which bind with ground substance proteins to form the extracellular matrix. Embedded within the cartilage matrix are chondrocytes, or cartilage cells, and the space they occupy are called lacunae (singular = lacuna). A layer of dense irregular connective tissue, the perichondrium, encapsulates the cartilage. Cartilaginous tissue is avascular, thus all nutrients need to diffuse through the matrix to reach the chondrocytes. This is a factor contributing to the very slow healing of cartilaginous tissues.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Supportive connective tissue
cartilage
hyaline – short, dispersed collagen fibres
strong & flexible 
e.g., ribcage, main part of nose, bone covering at moveable joints
makes up embryonic skeleton before bone formation
at ends of long bones, allowing growth, until adulthood
fibrocartilage
tough because of thick bundles of collagen fibres
e.g., knee and jaw joints, intervertebral discs
elastic
elastic + collagen fibres = rigid but elastic
e.g., external ear, tip of nose

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The three main types of cartilage tissue are hyaline cartilage, fibrocartilage, and elastic cartilage. 

Hyaline cartilage, the most common type of cartilage in the body, contains short and dispersed collagen fibres in the matrix. Both strong and flexible, the hyaline cartilage is found in the rib cage and nose and covers bones where they meet to form moveable joints. It makes up a template of the embryonic skeleton before bone formation. A plate of hyaline cartilage at the ends of bone allows continued growth until adulthood. 

Fibrocartilage is tough because it has thick bundles of collagen fibres dispersed through its matrix. The knee and jaw joints and the intervertebral discs are examples of fibrocartilage. 

Elastic cartilage contains elastic fibres as well as collagen. This tissue gives rigid support as well as elasticity. Tug gently at your ear lobes, and notice that the lobes return to their initial shape. The external ear contains elastic cartilage.

slides.title: Part 3. Connective tissue
slides.body:
Part 3. Connective tissue

Supportive connective tissue
bone
rigid extracellular matrix containing collagen fibres in mineralized ground substance (containing hydroxyapatite, a form of calcium phosphate)
collagen prevents brittleness and shattering, mineral prevents flexing
osteocytes (bone cells) located within lacunae (spaces in bone)
found in concentric circles around a central canal
highly vascularized – heals faster than cartilage

Compact bone & spongy bone. Credit: SEER, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Bone is the hardest connective tissue. It provides protection to internal organs and supports the body. Bone’s rigid extracellular matrix contains mostly collagen fibres embedded in a mineralized ground substance containing hydroxyapatite, a form of calcium phosphate. Both components of the matrix, organic and inorganic, contribute to the unusual properties of bone. Without collagen, bones would be brittle and shatter easily. Without mineral crystals, bones would flex and provide little support. Osteocytes, bone cells similar to chondrocytes, are located within lacunae—the small spaces in the bone tissue. These can be found in concentric circles around a central canal. Bone is a highly vascularized tissue. Because of this blood supply, and unlike cartilage, bone tissue can recover from injuries in a relatively short time.

Compact bone is solid and has great structural strength.

Cancellous bone (also known as trabecular or spongy bone) looks like a sponge under the microscope and contains empty spaces between trabeculae, or arches of bone proper. It is lighter than compact bone and found in the interior of some bones and at the end of long bones.

Fluid connective tissue: blood and lymph

Connective tissue examples

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Okay, so now we’ll finish our discussion of connective tissue with fluid connective tissue: blood and lymph.

Fluid connective tissue
cells circulate in a liquid extracellular matrix

Blood: A Fluid Connective Tissue. Blood is a fluid connective tissue containing erythrocytes and various types of leukocytes that circulate in a liquid extracellular matrix. LM × 1600. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In fluid connective tissues, cells circulate in a liquid extracellular matrix. The formed elements circulating in blood are all derived from hematopoietic stem cells (a type of multipotent adult stem cells) located in bone marrow. Erythrocytes, the formal name for red blood cells, transport oxygen and some carbon dioxide. Leukocytes, or white blood cells, are responsible for defending against potentially harmful microorganisms or molecules. Platelets are cell fragments involved in blood clotting.

Some white blood cells have the ability to cross the endothelial layer that lines blood vessels and enter adjacent tissues. Nutrients, salts, and wastes are dissolved in the liquid matrix, the plasma, and transported throughout the body.

Lymph also contains a liquid matrix and white blood cells, since, as just mentioned, they can migrate out of the blood; however lymph does not contain red blood cells or platelets. Lymphatic capillaries are extremely permeable, allowing larger molecules and excess fluid from interstitial spaces to enter the lymphatic vessels. Lymph drains into blood vessels, delivering molecules to the blood that could not otherwise directly enter the bloodstream. In this way, specialized lymphatic capillaries transport absorbed fats away from the intestine and deliver these molecules to the blood.

slides.title: Part 4. Muscle tissue

Part 4. Muscle tissue

Excitable – respond to stimulus
Contractile – shorten and generate pulling force
Some is voluntary, some involuntary
3 types: skeletal, cardiac, smooth

Comparison of structure and properties of muscle tissue types

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Muscle tissue is characterized by the property of allowing movement. Muscle cells are excitable; they respond to a stimulus. They are contractile, meaning they can shorten and generate a pulling force. When attached between two movable objects, lay say bones, contractions of the muscles cause the bones to move. Some muscle movement is voluntary, which means it is under conscious control. Other movements are involuntary, such as the contraction of the pupils of your eyes in bright light. Muscle tissue is classified into three types according to structure and function: skeletal, cardiac, and smooth.

slides.title: Part 4. Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 4. Muscle tissue

Skeletal – 40% of body mass!
striated – patterns of actin and myosin, and multinucleated
usually attached to bones
usually voluntary, sometimes involuntary (e.g., shivering for warmth), sometimes both (e.g., diaphragm)
Smooth – e.g., digestive, urinary, reproductive systems
not striated, uninucleate, spindle-shaped
involuntary
some types have intrinsic rhythms
some types electrically coupled
Cardiac

intrinsic rhythms
primarily involuntary
intercalated discs (synchrony)

Muscle Tissue. (a) Skeletal muscle cells have prominent striation and nuclei on their periphery. (b) Smooth muscle cells have a single nucleus and no visible striations.(c) Cardiac muscle cells appear striated and have a single nucleus. From top, LM × 1600, LM × 1600, LM × 1600. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Forty percent of body mass is made up of skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and its contraction allows for locomotion, facial expressions, posture, and other voluntary movements of the body. Apart from movement, skeletal muscles also generate heat as a byproduct of their contraction, both from friction and ATP hydrolysis, and thus participate in thermal homeostasis. Shivering is an involuntary contraction of skeletal muscles in response to lowered body temperature. 

Skeletal muscles are usually under voluntary control. The diaphragm is a bit of an exception. It is a skeletal muscle that helps with breathing, and it is under both voluntary and involuntary control.

Skeletal muscle tissue is arranged in bundles surrounded by connective tissue. Under the light microscope, its muscle cells—called muscle fibres or myocytes—appear striated, or striped, and with many nuclei squeezed along their length. The striation is due to the regular alternation of the contractile proteins actin and myosin, along with structural proteins that couple them to connective tissues. The multinucleation is a result of developmental fusion of many myoblasts to form each long muscle fibre. The number of muscle fibres in skeletal muscle remains relatively constant throughout life.

Smooth muscle tissue contraction is responsible for involuntary movements in internal organs. Smooth muscle tissue forms the contractile component of the digestive, urinary, and reproductive systems as well as the airways and blood vessels. Each smooth muscle fibre is spindle shaped (a little like a diamond) with a single nucleus and no visible striations.

Cardiac muscle forms the contractile walls of the heart. Like skeletal muscle, the cells of cardiac muscle, known as cardiomyocytes, appear striated under the microscope. Unlike skeletal muscle fibres, however, cardiomyocytes contain solely a single centrally located nucleus. A principal characteristic of cardiomyocytes is that they contract according to their own intrinsic rhythms, a characteristic that they share with some types of smooth muscle. Cardiomyocytes attach to one another with specialized cell junctions called intercalated discs. Attached cells form long, branching cardiac muscle fibres that are interconnected, mechanically and electrochemically, allowing the cells to work in a synchronized unison. The cardiac muscle of the heart pumps blood through the body and is primarily under involuntary control.

Part 5. Nervous tissue

The Neuron. The cell body of a neuron, also called the soma, contains the nucleus and mitochondria. The dendrites transfer the nerve impulse to the soma. The axon carries the action potential away to another excitable cell. LM × 1600. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Nervous tissue is characterized as being excitable and capable of sending and receiving electrochemical signals that provide the body with information. Two main classes of cells make up nervous tissue: the neuron and neuroglia. 

Neurons propagate information via electrochemical impulses, called action potentials, which are biochemically linked to the release of chemical signals, neurotransmitters. 

Neuroglia play an essential role in supporting neurons and modulating their information propagation. Some neuroglia also have immune functions.

The presence of the nervous tissue throughout the body and its organization allow it to receive, integrate and provide information to the entire body. This ensures that appropriate responses can occur among all body systems within an intact organism, both under normal conditions as well as during times of stress.

slides.body:
Part 5. Nervous tissue

Neurons
form matches function
dendrites – thin extensions that receive information
cell soma (cell body)
axons – long protrusion from soma
can by wrapped in myelin to speed electrical transmission
synapse – the gap between axon and another neuron or target (e.g., muscle or gland)
electrical impulse down axon leads to NT release within synapse
triggers electrical change in post-synaptic cell

The Neuron. The cell body of a neuron, also called the soma, contains the nucleus and mitochondria. The dendrites transfer the nerve impulse to the soma. The axon carries the action potential away to another excitable cell. LM × 1600. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Neurons display distinctive morphology, well suited to their role as conducting cells, with three main parts. The cell body, or cell soma, includes most of the cytoplasm, the organelles, and the nucleus. Dendrites, which are parts of a neuron that receive information, branch off from the cell body and appear as thin extensions. A long “tail,” the axon, extends from the neuron body and can be wrapped in an insulating layer known as myelin, formed by accessory neuroglia. Myelin helps increase the speed of neural transmissions. The synapse is the gap between nerve cells, or between a nerve cell and its target, for example, a muscle or a gland. An electrical impulse in one cell leads to chemical signaling compounds known as neurotransmitters being released from its axon terminal, into the synapse. They diffuse across the synapse, bind to receptors on the other side, and again trigger an electrical change in that post-synaptic cell.

more support roles then discovered (covered in NS unit)
recent research suggest even greater roles

The Neuron. The cell body of a neuron, also called the soma, contains the nucleus and mitochondria. The dendrites transfer the nerve impulse to the soma. THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Neuroglia, or glial cells, have historically been characterized as having a simple support role. The word “glia” comes from the Greek word for glue. However, recent research is shedding light on the more complex role of neuroglia in the function of the brain and nervous system. We will discuss these roles in more detail in the nervous system unit.
